strengths: Residents remain relatively calm without panic or anxiety despite ongoing threat
No acute psychological distress as experienced immediately after October 7th
concerns: Significant disconnect between government messaging (Hezbollah deterred) and actual threat reality over past two weeks
Sharp decline in state support and attention compared to previous round—residents feel neglected despite continued emergency status
Growing frustration that visibility and tangible government assistance have disappeared
components.narrative: The community narrative has shifted from panic to cautious fatigue. While residents are not in acute distress, they report surprise and disappointment at contradictions between official narratives of Hezbollah deterrence and observable enemy activity, combined with a dramatic reduction in state support compared to the previous emergency round. This creates a sense of abandonment despite ongoing threat.

strengths: 16 public shelters available in the settlement
Approximately 86.7% of households (estimated based on ~30 without bomb shelters out of ~150 typical homes) have protected rooms or access to shelters
concerns: 30 households entirely lack domestic bomb shelters (mamad)
2 of 16 shelters are non-functional; 2 families are living in shelters full-time
Elderly population faces severe mobility constraints in reaching shelters during alert periods
components.narrative: Protection infrastructure exists but contains critical gaps. While most households have shelter access, approximately 30 families are completely unprotected, and elderly residents with mobility limitations struggle to reach shelters in the required timeframe. Two non-operational shelters and families permanently living in shelters indicate shelter distress.

strengths: Some recreational activities continue in limited, short-duration formats per guidelines
concerns: Complete suspension of formal schooling for the duration of emergency
Recreation and community programs severely restricted to minimal, brief sessions
Functional continuity severely disrupted—adults recalled to workplace while schools remain closed, creating childcare crises and conflicting obligations
Two weeks into emergency with no clarity on timeline for normalcy; residents experiencing prolonged operational dysfunction
components.narrative: Daily life has collapsed into minimal functionality. Schools are entirely closed while parents are expected to return to work, creating structural impossibility for working families. Brief, limited recreational programs do not constitute meaningful functional continuity, and the open-ended emergency duration compounds strain on household operations and work resumption.

strengths: Active readiness unit (29 community volunteers) mobilized and functioning
Municipal leadership distributing presence surveys to track population and household status
concerns: Gap in volunteer roster completeness—not all community members with capacity are formally enlisted
No neighborhood heads appointed (municipality leadership states no need), limiting localized resource coordination
Limited evidence of CSO/community organization infrastructure being fully activated
components.narrative: The community has basic volunteer mobilization through the readiness unit, but community capital extraction is incomplete. The absence of neighborhood leadership structures and gaps in volunteer enumeration suggest untapped local resource coordination capacity that could strengthen mutual aid networks.

strengths: Active, regular communication—WhatsApp emergency groups, weekly council updates with head-of-council messages
Systematic presence tracking mechanism (survey system) implemented to monitor population status
Leadership demonstrating proactive outreach and information distribution
concerns: Messages focus on logistics and information but no evidence of strategic, forward-looking communication addressing residents' psychological needs or timeline clarity
No mention of leadership engagement with elderly or at-risk population needs despite 15% elderly demographic
components.narrative: Municipal leadership is functionally active in information dissemination and administrative tracking. Communication channels are established and used regularly, but messaging appears transactional rather than reassuring or strategic. Leadership visibility on broader community resilience—particularly for vulnerable populations—is not evident.

strengths: Informal activities continue in community framework, albeit in restricted formats
Basic social cohesion mechanism intact—residents remain engaged in limited collective activities
concerns: Activities severely constrained to brief, minimal sessions due to alert protocols
No evidence of expanded mutual aid, neighboring support, or organized community solidarity initiatives
Limited visibility into informal social bonding or morale-sustaining efforts
components.narrative: Community belonging remains latent but is not being actively cultivated. While informal activities technically continue, the restrictive format and brief duration mean they provide minimal emotional or social reinforcement during a prolonged emergency. Solidarity is not being actively mobilized or reinforced.

strengths: Municipality aware of at-risk population composition (15% elderly, mixed secular-majority community)
Social services department exists and presence (though not directly interviewed)
concerns: Elderly population (15% of residents) faces severe protection and mobility barriers—cannot safely reach shelters in alert timeframe; living conditions in unprotected homes create ongoing vulnerability
No documented welfare department or psychosocial support response to emergency-induced stress
No adapted services or support plans for elderly residents or families with young children in prolonged high-alert state
Generator shortage (single generator serving community center and one shelter) leaves residents dependent on supplemental oxygen without adequate power backup solution
components.narrative: At-risk populations—particularly elderly residents and families with small children—face compounded vulnerability. Elderly residents cannot physically access shelter protection in required timeframes and live in unprotected housing, while families with young children are confined continuously without respite programs. No coordinated welfare or mental health response is documented despite two weeks of continuous emergency stress. Specific medical vulnerability (oxygen-dependent residents) remains unresolved.
